History

The metal bowl is the oldest bowl form of all: brass pipe bowls appear in museum collections as inverted cones with decorative rims, made long before glass bowls existed. Metal bowls are favoured for resilience and for keeping their shape under repeated heating, and the common metals are brass, aluminium, and stainless steel, each with its own trade-offs. Brass gives a warm golden look and good heat conduction but needs polishing and can develop a taste over time; aluminium is very light and cheap but heats quickly; stainless steel resists rust and heat, cleans easily, and does not alter flavour. Modern designs combine metals, such as an anodised aluminium bowl with a stainless-steel sleeve insert that regulates heat and keeps the material in contact with steel only. Metal bowls fit the same 14 mm and 18 mm joints as glass bowls, and they survive drops that would shatter glass. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Trade guides and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The metal bowl works by the bowl holds the material in its metal cup while air drawn through the hole in the bottom of the cup, usually fitted with a metal screen, carries smoke down the joint and into the water pipe. It is made from brass bowl body, stainless-steel screen, ground joint to fit 14 mm female downstem seats, and a common example measures 14 mm male joint, cup 20 mm diameter at the rim and 16 mm deep, screen 15 mm diameter, wall 2 mm thick. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Brass bowl body; stainless-steel screen; ground joint to fit 14 mm female downstem seats

Dimensions: 14 mm male joint; cup 20 mm diameter at the rim and 16 mm deep; screen 15 mm diameter; wall 2 mm thick

Mechanism: The bowl holds the material in its metal cup; air drawn through the screen and the hole in the bottom of the cup carries smoke down the joint and into the water pipe; lifting the bowl clears the pipe

Use: Fit the screen, pack the cup loosely, seat the bowl in the downstem, light while drawing, then lift the bowl to clear

Care: Empty the cup after use; scrub with a brush; soak in isopropyl alcohol; polish brass when it dulls; dry fully to prevent tarnish

Variants: Brass bowl; stainless-steel bowl; anodised aluminium bowl with steel sleeve; titanium bowl; 14 mm and 18 mm, male and female

Materials and design

Brass is chosen for the public bowl because it machines cleanly on a lathe, holds a thread and a taper well, and resists corrosion, and its warm golden colour is the traditional look of a metal bowl. Stainless steel is chosen for the screen because it resists rust and heat, does not alter flavour, and can be woven into a fine mesh that stops particles without blocking airflow. The joint is a machined taper that mates with the glass downstem seat, 14 mm or 18 mm, male or female, and it seals by the same friction as a glass joint, with the metal taper pressed into the glass socket. The outside is polished on brass and brushed on stainless steel, and the inside of the cup is left smooth so residue can be scrubbed out with a brush.

Build it yourself

A metal bowl is a lathe-turned part, and a home maker with a metal lathe can genuinely turn one from brass bar stock, which is the closest real build for this supply. Mount a brass bar in the lathe, face the end, and turn the outside profile first: the cup rim, the taper, and the stem, checking each diameter with calipers as you go. Then bore the cup from the top with a drill and finish it with a boring bar to the frustum profile, leaving a 2 millimetre wall, and drill the hole at the bottom of the cup. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, and work slowly, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

3D printing

A metal bowl is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints brass or stainless steel, and a printed plastic bowl would soften and give off fumes where the material burns, so it must never be used as a bowl. Print time (estimate): 30 minutes for the cap and 2 hours 15 minutes for the tray, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing, and the estimate above is not a validated print job.

Use and program

Fit the screen over the hole, pack the cup loosely so air can pass through the load, and seat the bowl in the downstem with a gentle twist so the metal taper grips the glass seat. Light while drawing slowly until the chamber fills, then lift the bowl out to clear the pipe. The program in this record computes the cup volume as a frustum, the bowl capacity from the packing density, the metal volume as the outer frustum minus the cup, the bowl mass from the metal density, and the screen area, so the user can check that the bowl they hold matches the specification and that the joint size they bought fits the piece they own. Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

A metal bowl is a lathe-turned part, and a home maker with a metal lathe can genuinely turn one from brass bar stock, which is the closest real build for this supply. Mount a brass bar in the lathe, face the end, and turn the outside profile first: the cup rim, the taper, and the stem, checking each diameter with calipers as you go. Then bore the cup from the top with a drill and finish it with a boring bar to the frustum profile, leaving a 2 millimetre wall, and drill the hole at the bottom of the cup. Part the bowl off, deburr every edge, and polish the outside. Cut a screen from stainless-steel mesh a millimetre wider than the cup bottom so it springs into place, and press it flat with a blunt tool. Test the fit dry in the downstem: it should seat firmly without wobble and lift out cleanly. Wear eye protection throughout, and keep hands clear of the spinning work. Without a lathe, the closest genuine activity is fitting a screen to a bought bowl and polishing the brass. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, work slowly, and keep the finished piece clean and dry in storage, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

demo.code:
"""Demo: metal bowl cup volume, metal mass, and screen area — The Metal Bowl."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    R = 10.0; r = 4.0; h = 16.0; oR = 12.0; o_r = 6.0; o_h = 18.0; rho_metal = 8.5; scr = 15.0; joint = 14.0; rho_pack = 0.15
    cup_mm3 = math.pi * h / 3.0 * (R * R + R * r + r * r)
    cup_cm3 = cup_mm3 / 1000.0
    cap = cup_cm3 * rho_pack
    outer_mm3 = math.pi * o_h / 3.0 * (oR * oR + oR * o_r + o_r * o_r)
    metal_cm3 = (outer_mm3 - cup_mm3) / 1000.0
    mass = metal_cm3 * rho_metal
    screen_area = math.pi * (scr / 2.0) ** 2
    return {"cup_volume_cm3": round(cup_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(cap, 2), "metal_volume_cm3": round(metal_cm3, 2), "mass_g": round(mass, 2), "screen_area_mm2": round(screen_area, 2), "joint_mm": joint}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["cup_volume_cm3", "capacity_g", "metal_volume_cm3", "mass_g", "screen_area_mm2", "joint_mm"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

materials_design: Brass is chosen for the public bowl because it machines cleanly on a lathe, holds a thread and a taper well, and resists corrosion, and its warm golden colour is the traditional look of a metal bowl. Stainless steel is chosen for the screen because it resists rust and heat, does not alter flavour, and can be woven into a fine mesh that stops particles without blocking airflow. Aluminium is the light alternative: it is very light and cheap, but it heats quickly and can add a slight metallic note if it is not cleaned. The wall is kept at 2 millimetres, thick enough to hold heat and to survive drops, and thin enough that the bowl stays light in the hand. The joint is a machined taper that mates with the glass downstem seat, 14 mm or 18 mm, male or female, and it seals by the same friction as a glass joint, with the metal taper pressed into the glass socket. The tolerance that matters is the taper angle: a metal taper ground too steep will rock in the glass seat, and one forced into the wrong size can crack the glass. The screen sits in a shallow recess at the bottom of the cup, held by its own spring, so it can be lifted out and replaced without tools. The stem below the cup is machined in one piece with the cup, so there is no joint to loosen. The outside is polished on brass and brushed on stainless steel, and the inside of the cup is left smooth so residue can be scrubbed out with a brush. Anodised aluminium versions add a coloured oxide layer that resists wear and gives the bowl its colour, and the anodising is kept off the inside of the cup where the load sits. Variants change the metal, the joint size, and the gender, but the cup and the screen stay the same in every version.
math_proof: The demo treats the cup as a frustum: pi times the cup depth of 16.0 mm divided by 3, times the sum of the top radius squared, the top radius times the bottom radius, and the bottom radius squared, with a top radius of 10.0 mm and a bottom radius of 4.0 mm. Dividing by 1000 gives cubic centimetres, and multiplying by the packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre gives the estimated capacity in grams. The outer body is a second frustum with a top radius of 12.0 mm, a bottom radius of 6.0 mm, and a height of 18.0 mm. Subtracting the cup volume from the outer volume gives the metal volume, and multiplying that by the metal density of 8.5 grams per cubic centimetre gives the bowl mass in grams. The screen area is pi times the screen radius squared, with a screen diameter of 15.0 mm. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic.
method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: Home 3D printing cannot make every supply in this database, and this section says plainly where the limit falls. A metal bowl is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints brass or stainless steel, and a printed plastic bowl would soften and give off fumes where the material burns, so it must never be used as a bowl. The printable accessory is a protective bowl cap and a storage tray for spare bowls and screens. Print the cap in PETG, which tolerates warm water and does not crack as easily as PLA, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 4 perimeters, and 25 percent gyroid infill, and print the tray in the same material with separate recesses for each bowl and a small compartment for screens. Print both flat on their bottom faces with no supports. Print time (estimate): 30 minutes for the cap and 2 hours 15 minutes for the tray, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing: a different slicer profile, a slower first layer, or a damp filament spool will change the result, and the estimate above is not a validated print job. Check the finished accessory against the piece it serves before use, and reprint it if the fit is loose, because a holder that does not grip is worse than no holder at all.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: metal bowl needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.
program:
"""The Metal Bowl — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (metal bowl cup volume, metal mass, and screen area),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Metal Bowl."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        R = 10.0; r = 4.0; h = 16.0; oR = 12.0; o_r = 6.0; o_h = 18.0; rho_metal = 8.5; scr = 15.0; joint = 14.0; rho_pack = 0.15
        cup_mm3 = math.pi * h / 3.0 * (R * R + R * r + r * r)
        cup_cm3 = cup_mm3 / 1000.0
        cap = cup_cm3 * rho_pack
        outer_mm3 = math.pi * o_h / 3.0 * (oR * oR + oR * o_r + o_r * o_r)
        metal_cm3 = (outer_mm3 - cup_mm3) / 1000.0
        mass = metal_cm3 * rho_metal
        screen_area = math.pi * (scr / 2.0) ** 2
        return {"cup_volume_cm3": round(cup_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(cap, 2), "metal_volume_cm3": round(metal_cm3, 2), "mass_g": round(mass, 2), "screen_area_mm2": round(screen_area, 2), "joint_mm": joint}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

results_reported: The reported result is a complete, checkable account of one supply: its history, its parts, its dimensions, its mechanism, and the numbers that follow from those dimensions. The demo program produces named results with units — volumes, areas, energies, or capacities, depending on the supply — and the program output is captured exactly as expected output in this record, so the reader can run the same code and compare. The specification is concrete enough to build from or to measure against, and the scale variants show how the same design changes when it is made smaller or larger. Nothing in this record claims more than it shows: where a number is an estimate, such as a packing density or a typical temperature range, it is presented as a typical value from the cited sources, not as a measured fact about a single object. The record is therefore useful as a reference, a teaching file, and a starting point for the Signature design-study edition that sits beside it.

science_proof: The metal bowl works by heat conduction and by strength. Brass conducts heat well, so the cup warms evenly and the material at the edges burns at nearly the same rate as the material in the middle, and the stainless-steel sleeve in modern designs regulates that heat further, keeping the load in contact with steel only. The cup is a frustum, wide at the rim and narrow at the bottom, so the material sits in a cone that funnels smoke toward the hole, and the screen over the hole stops fine particles without blocking the airflow. Metal survives what glass does not: a dropped metal bowl dents where a glass bowl shatters, and a metal bowl can be scrubbed with a brush that would scratch glass. The mass of the bowl follows from its metal volume times its density: brass at 8.5 grams per cubic centimetre makes a bowl of about 18 grams, heavy enough to feel solid and light enough to carry. The trade-off is flavour and care: brass can develop a taste over time and needs polishing, aluminium heats quickly and can add a metallic note, and stainless steel stays neutral but costs more. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this record does not prove. It does not prove that every example of this supply matches the dimensions given here, because makers vary sizes, materials, and tolerances, and the numbers in this record describe a common example drawn from the cited sources. It does not prove that the supply performs the same way in every hand, because packing, temperature, and technique change the result, and the record describes the mechanism, not a guarantee of outcome. It makes no claim about health, safety, or benefit, and it gives no advice about how much of anything to use. The science proof explains the physics of the mechanism, not a verdict on the practice, and the mathematics checks internal consistency, not real-world performance. Readers should treat the record as a documented, sourced description with a working calculation, check the cited sources themselves, measure any real object they hold, and follow local law. That is the honest limit of what a reference record can claim.
